chapter: Dew Drop and the club scene
title: The Dew Drop: Frank Painia's club, acts and hotel
summary: After the war the Dew Drop drew national acts; Larry McKinley's promoting costs; competition with the Robin Hood; Painia's hotel and restaurant gave him the whole package.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: ...his... Right after the soldiers started coming home, and then some soldiers were passing through, and like we said, things were not as integrated as they are now, and people wanted to... People had a few money. Some people were covered being, uh, turned loose and normal with three, four, five, six hundred dollars, which was a lot of money. Remember, Coca-Cola was 25 cents, uh, Coca-Cola was five cents a bottle. You could get a half a pint of liquor for 45 cents, along with a seven-up of Coke and a pitcher of water. Uh, you lived good. And if you spent a dollar, boy, you were really big time in the place, because you got two half pints, or either you got your pint of liquor for about 95 cents or whatever. But here is the dew drop. Here was Frank Panae exploring new horizons, places where he had never been before, but he was trying, because why? He wanted to make sure that his club, in the name of the dew drop, which was two little words, but it became nationwide. Why? Because you're in a major city. Everything is segregated. You got your radio stations blasting the dew drop every day on the air. You got Ray Charles coming in. You got Big Joe Turner coming in. You got Nat King Cole coming in. You got James Brown coming in. You got the Blazers coming in. You got so many different acts and so many different names. Little Miss Cornshuck's one of my favorite people. Anytime she was there, I was always there. She was funny, but she could sing. So all in all, the dew drop imported more out of town name talent between 1945 and 1960 than any other person in town, other than the promoters like Jackson, Rip Roberts, or maybe some of the other promoters like Larry McKinley and a few others. Now, Larry McKinley promoted more big time acts, continuous, than any other promoter that we have until all of a sudden the entertainers themselves, they wanted a special limousine for themselves, a special limousine for their lady friend, or then they wanted fruit, a fruit bowl behind stage with concession of all kinds of sandwiches, and they wanted high powered liquors and wines for a special party for their traveling group. So Larry said he had to get out of that sometimes, you know, beside paying the taxes that the city wanted for the auditorium or city park. He would have to come up with an extra five or ten thousand dollars almost for these two limousines and also for this fruit salad, for this food, and for all this extra liquor. And then they got some guys who probably never drank the most expensive brands, but when they're on the road with Al Green or if they're on the road with Big Joe Turner, they want to be seen drinking the best of everything and eating the best of everything and throwing the best of everything away. That's what's saying. So Larry said we got to get away from that. But Frank Pena, like I said, the only competition that he had at that particular time was probably the Robin Hood with Bennett Ross who on a day to day basis were, well they were just about a half a mile apart, but they were the very best of friends. Sometimes they would swap talent. Sometimes Paul Gaten would probably leave the Robin Hood and go play Frank Pena, but his mainstay was strictly with the Robin Hood. That's where I first saw him, he and Annie Laurie. And Paul Gaten was a tremendous talent. And like I said, Frank Pena knew how to put things together. He knew how to spend money. And he had an advantage by having a hotel in the back with about 20 to 30 rooms. See, he could take care of a band, take care of the entertainer, and they didn't have to worry about going downtown because they couldn't go downtown anyway because everything was segregated. And so Frank had the advantage over most clubs because he had the facility for the entertainment. He had the facility for people to relax themselves. He had the facility for people to relax themselves. He had the restaurant and the lounge there. What else more did you want? Because you had it all for his hand right in front of you right then and there. And so Frank had the advantage over most clubs, because he had the facility for the entertainment, he had the facility for people to relax themselves, he had the restaurant and the lounge there, what else more did you want? Because you had it all for his hand right in front of you, right then and there.
He had the whole package. He had the package.
